chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The real estate market moves in cycles: seller-favourable periods, buyer-favourable periods, and transitions. Understanding these dynamics in Greater Montréal helps you decide with judgment rather than following the collective emotion.

This guide explains the market's phases, the indicators to watch, and how to act according to the context — without trying to perfectly “time” the market.

Informational content. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

The market moves in cycles: seller-favourable periods, buyer-favourable periods, and transitions. This guide explains how to recognize the type of market, the factors that move it, the indicators to follow and how to act without trying to guess the peak.

The message: decide with judgment, according to your situation, rather than following the collective emotion.

chapters.title: Buyer's market, seller's market
chapters.html:
Recognizing which market you're in.

The market swings between two extremes, with a balance in the middle:

  • Seller's market: demand exceeds supply. Few properties, quick sales, possible bidding wars.
  • Buyer's market: supply exceeds demand. More choice, longer timelines, downward negotiation.
  • Balanced market: between the two.

The key index is the number of months of inventory: how long it would take to sell off all the properties for sale at the current pace.

The most telling index is the number of months of inventory: low, it signals a seller's market (quick sales, bidding wars); high, a buyer's market (choice, negotiation). Don't rely on national headlines: one neighbourhood can favour sellers while another favours buyers.

Emilie's tip

Don't rely on national headlines: the market is local. One Montréal neighbourhood can favour sellers while another favours buyers. Look at YOUR area's numbers.

chapters.title: The factors that move the market
chapters.html:
Understanding the forces at play.

No single factor tells everything; it's their combination that shapes the market:

  • Interest rates: they strongly influence borrowing capacity and therefore demand.
  • Economy and employment: confidence, incomes, migration.
  • Supply: housing starts, land availability, regulation.
  • Demographics and areas: some neighbourhoods stay sought-after whatever the cycle.

Understanding these levers helps you interpret what you see rather than react in the heat of the moment.

No single factor tells everything: interest rates (the #1 lever on demand), economy and employment, supply (housing starts, regulation), demographics and area appeal. It's their combination that shapes the market. When rates rise, pressure on prices often eases.

Emilie's tip

When rates rise, borrowing capacity drops and pressure on prices often eases. When they fall, it's the opposite. Follow rates: it's the number-one factor.

chapters.title: The indicators to watch
chapters.html:
Reading the market with numbers.

To situate yourself, a few simple, public indicators are worth more than impressions:

  • Months of inventory: low = seller's market, high = buyer's market.
  • Average time to sell: how many days on market.
  • Sold price / asking price ratio: above 100% signals bidding wars.
  • Median price by property type and by area.

Tracked over time, these numbers tell the trend better than a single spectacular sale.

To situate yourself, a few public indicators are worth more than impressions: months of inventory, average time to sell, sold/asking price ratio (above 100% = bidding wars), median price by type and area. Tracked over time, they tell the trend better than a spectacular sale.

Emilie's tip

A single house sold very high (or very low) doesn't make a trend. Look at the median price and the time to sell over several months: that's where the real market story is.

chapters.title: Acting without trying to guess the peak
chapters.objective: Deciding according to your needs, not speculation.
chapters.html:
Deciding according to your needs, not speculation.

No one “times” the market perfectly — not the experts, not the banks. For most households, the right decision depends mainly:

  • on their personal situation (need, stability, capacity);
  • on their holding horizon.

Real estate generally rewards patience and long-term holding, which smooth out the cycles. Waiting for “the perfect bottom” often means missing good opportunities.

No one “times” the market perfectly — not the experts, not the banks. For most households, the right decision depends mainly on their situation (need, stability, capacity) and their horizon. Patience and long holding smooth out the cycles.

Emilie's tip

The best question isn't “is it the right time for the market?” but “is it the right time for ME?” A real need and a long holding almost always beat speculation.

chapters.title: Greater Montréal: markets within the market
chapters.html:
Nuancing by area.

The “Montréal market” doesn't really exist: it's a mosaic of local markets with distinct dynamics.

  • Property type: condos, plexes and single-family homes don't move at the same pace.
  • Area: the core, the crowns, the suburbs and the regions each have their own logic.
  • Price segment: entry-level and high-end react differently to rates.

Comparing your project to the right local data avoids false conclusions drawn from too-broad statistics.

The “Montréal market” doesn't really exist: it's a mosaic of local markets (property type, area, price segment) with distinct dynamics. Comparing your project to the right local data — the recent comparables of YOUR area — avoids false conclusions.

Emilie's tip

Ask your broker for the comparable sales of the last three to six months in YOUR area and for YOUR property type. It's a hundred times more useful than a provincial statistic.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Identify the current type of market in my area.
  2. Follow inventory, timelines and the sold/asking price ratio.

Within 30 days

  1. Understand the effect of rates on my project.
  2. Clarify my needs and my horizon.

Next

  1. Decide according to my situation, with Emilie's insight on the local market.

To read the market

  1. Identify my area's type of market (inventory, timelines, price ratio).
  2. Decide according to my needs and horizon, with recent local comparables.
